changes.after: Count Rust text by bytes or by Unicode scalar values.

before: A single-quoted char such as 'é' is a Unicode scalar value, not merely one UTF-8 byte and not a complete grapheme cluster in every case.
String::from("é") creates an owned growable String. A double-quoted string literal provides an &str borrowed text view; full borrowing rules follow later.

String.len counts UTF-8 bytes. chars().count counts Unicode scalar values. Neither is a universal count of user-perceived characters.

text.chars() borrows the text and returns an iterator that yields Unicode scalar values. Calling count() on that iterator consumes it and returns the number of yielded scalars; it is not a byte-count or grapheme-segmentation operation.
The sample é uses two UTF-8 bytes and one scalar value. ASCII A uses one byte and one scalar value.
Expected output or behavior: 2 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare byte length and scalar counts for another bounded literal. Do not assume either counts grapheme clusters. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Unicode assigns numbers to text symbols. A Rust `char`, written in single quotes such as `'é'`, holds one Unicode scalar value. That value may need several bytes when stored as UTF-8 text.
A double-quoted literal provides a borrowed text view, `&str`. `String::from("é")` creates a String that owns its text and can grow. Later lessons explain ownership and borrowing.
A byte is a small unit of stored data. `text.len()` counts UTF-8 bytes. `text.chars()` visits scalar values, and `count()` counts how many it visits.
This `é` uses two UTF-8 bytes and one scalar value. Some letters as you see them use more than one scalar value, so neither count always equals visible letters.
The screen shows `2 1`: two bytes, then one scalar value.
Change the text to `"A"`. This letter uses one byte and one scalar value.

before.explanation: The two counts coincide for ASCII but differ for the original sample.

after.question: If the text changes to "A", what appears?
choices: 2 1, because every String takes two bytes.
1 2, because A has two scalar values.
1 1, because A uses one byte and one scalar value.
after.explanation: Both counts are 1 for A. Other text can give different counts.
